content.thinking:
I'm planning out the chopper's proportions and dimensions—wheel sizes, wheelbase, and frame height—before working out the joint hierarchy starting from the root frame.

I'm structuring the skeleton with steering, wheel, and kickstand joints, then designing a helper function to build spoke geometry as oriented cylinders between hub and rim points, merged efficiently for performance.

For the wheels, I'm positioning a torus tire and a slightly smaller silver rim torus in the correct orientation, plus a hub cylinder rotated to align with the axle, and considering adding a thin brake disc with small boxes to simulate slots.

For tread detail, I'm painting the tire surface using its UV coordinates to generate a chevron zigzag pattern between two tire tones. Now I'm laying out the chassis in side view, placing front and rear wheel centers and giving the rear tire a thicker tube for a wider stance.

For the raked fork geometry, I'm positioning the head tube and tracing fork tubes down to the front axle, calculating the rake angle from the vertical and horizontal offsets—aiming for a realistic chopper-style angle closer to 38 degrees rather than the steeper 44-45 I first got.

Settling on head at [0,1.05,0.5] and axle at [0,0.35,1.1], giving about 40.6° rake. Now mapping out the main frame: downtube from the head to the engine mount area, with the backbone running from the head toward the seat region.

Laying out the rear hardtail rails to the rear axle, the seat rails, a tank loft along the backbone, the seat position, and a rear fender arc. For the skeleton, I'm planning a root frame joint, a steer joint at the head pointed toward the front axle, hinge joints for both wheels, plus a kickstand and brake/clutch levers, keeping the joint set minimal but functional before I move on to assigning weights to each part.

Now I'm defining the color palette with teal, orange, steel, chrome, and dark tones for a clean Overwatch-style finish rather than cel-shaded, then setting up paint functions to add orange panel sectors on the tank loft symmetrically on both sides.

Still working out the tank loft geometry, placing stations along the z-axis with varying widths and heights to shape the body, and positioning the backbone tube beneath the top surface.

For the engine, I'm laying out a V-twin: a dark steel crankcase box as the base, with two angled cylinders running up-forward and up-back to form the V, each with thin disc fins stacked along their length to simulate cooling fins, plus head covers. I'm checking that the tank's underside clearance and cylinder positions don't collide, and noting the V-twin cylinders sit in the fore-aft plane of the bike rather than side to side.

Now I'm adding a lathed primary cover disc on the right side with a rivet ring, then routing the exhaust pipes as curved sweeps from each cylinder's exhaust port down and back along the frame, with the pipe radius widening near the tail to form a muffler bulge before capping off with a dark tip.

I'm checking clearance between the muffler and rear wheel, confirming the pipe sits beside the tire without overlapping, then sketching a rigid hardtail rear frame with seat stays running from the mid-frame down to the rear axle, plus a sprocket cylinder and chain rods on the left side for the drivetrain.

Now I'm working out the chain path connecting the engine's output sprocket to the rear wheel sprocket, placing top and bottom chain lines between them, then moving to the fork design with chrome upper stanchions and teal lower tubes running from the steering crown down to the front axle, plus a triple tree crown box joining them.

Positioning the headlight next: a flattened sphere oriented forward with a chrome ring torus around the lens, mounted on the steer bone between the fork tubes, and I'm checking the geometry so it lines up properly with the fork's position at the front of the frame.

Now I'm sketching the ape hanger handlebars with a curved path rising from the crown up to high grips, mirrored for both sides, with black rubber grips capping the ends.

Then I move to mirrors—using a faceted octahedron scaled to a flattened diamond shape for that Overwatch-style look—and set up the lever joints attaching to the steering bone, before starting on the front wheel's brake disc assembly.

Working out the fork tube, disc, and caliper placement...

I'm reconsidering the fender shape -- a linear taper section won't map cleanly onto the sweep's frame since I'm unsure which axis the binormal and normal align to along an arc in the YZ plane, so I'm weighing a simpler fallback of scaling a partial torus instead.

Switching to a partial Torus (radius .41, tube .03) scaled along one axis to flatten it into a wide band, then figuring out the rotation needed so the arc sits centered at the top with its axis running along world X.

Working out the quaternion combination for arc orientation... I need to rotate by the Z offset first to position the arc start, then apply the Y rotation, multiplying qY by qZ in that order. For the front fender, I'm figuring out the angular span so it wraps from the front-lower area (around φ=155°) to the rear-upper area (around φ=40°).

Setting fender parameters now: front fender gets radius 0.40R with start angle 35° and arc span 120°, using 4 radial segments for a flatter torus profile and 14 tubular segments. For the rear fender I'm using similar proportions but shifted toward the back, and considering adding a thin orange trim torus but holding off since local X scaling isn't straightforward with the radial segments.

Now I'm planning the seat as a teardrop loft with a checkered quilt pattern using paint logic based on floor divisions of position, running the seat stations from the front down to the rear with tapering width and height. I'm also sketching in a small glowing red tail light box near the rear fender end.

Then I'm placing foot pegs on rods and a kickstand joint angled down and outward, and working out wheel geometry so the bike actually rests on the ground — tire radius and tube thickness determine where the wheel centers need to sit vertically.

Setting the fork axle to the adjusted width value, then adding tank details: a small gauge console, a chrome fuel cap cylinder positioned near the tank top, and figuring out the tank's vertical top bounds from its center heights. I'm deciding to skip the kicker and oil tank details for now.

Next I'm placing a teal-and-orange battery box between the seat and engine, then working out orange hexagonal decal panels extruded onto the tank's curved sides, calculating the tank's half-width at its widest point to position the hex outlines so they sit flush against the surface with a slight protrusion.

I'm simplifying the paint scheme to keep the orange facets but swap the hex decal for a darker steel-colored emblem with an orange rim, and setting frame tube radii for the backbone, downtube, and cradle running from the headstock down through the engine mounts.

Now I'm working out the head tube geometry: computing the fork's steering axis direction, then placing the crown and lower tree above and below the head tube center along that axis, with fork tubes spanning down to the axle on either side.

Checking the rake angle by verifying the axle's vertical and horizontal offsets from the head tube center, then designing the handlebar riser clamp boxes, chrome rim toruses, hub cylinders, and alternating spokes connecting hub to rim for each wheel.

Writing the geometry merge helper...

I'm scaling the rear tire tread wider via the tube's z-axis, and recalling how Three.js builds UV coordinates around a torus's tubular and radial segments to properly map tire tread texture.

Still working out the chevron pattern...

Positioning the speedometer housing on the tank front, using a small circle texture for the gauge face and figuring out coordinates near the top of the tank around z .5 for proper placement.

Now I'm shaping the headlight: a front-facing circular lens with a grid texture and strong glow, paired with a scaled sphere for the bucket housing and a rim torus, adjusting sizes so the lens sits just inside the bucket's front edge.

Adjusting fork geometry to fit snugly against the headlight bucket, then adding orange banded accents to the fork lowers using color sweeps along the tube.

Now I'm adding small details like axle nuts, rear fender struts, foot peg controls, and a curved sissy bar backrest sweeping from the rear frame upward.

I'm estimating the final part count around 120, adding rivet rows, primary-cover bolt rings, and oil lines, then starting to write the helper functions for vectors and cylinder geometry.

Still writing geometry helpers...

Still working out the rim geometry...

Still placing disc and caliper geometry...

Mapping out the rear sprocket as a flat-sided cylinder standing in for gear teeth, plus a matching rear brake disc on the opposite side. I'm standardizing wheel-related parts to use cylinder geometry with built-in orientation rather than separate rotation transforms, and now moving to fender placement using partial torus arcs with quaternion rotation for positioning.

Checking clearances: the tire's outer radius fits inside the fender's inner radius, so there's no overlap. I'm considering whether to add support stays connecting the fender to the fork or axle, but deciding to skip the extra mounting brackets for simplicity and move on to the rear fender.

Positioning the rear fender arc from 20° to 145° so it wraps properly over the back tire, then placing the tail light at the rear low point with a glow-red box, plus a small license plate.

Now I'm adding the oil tank as a teal box with an orange stripe on the right side, and an air cleaner cap on the left between the engine cylinders, chrome-colored, sized to fit without overlapping. Then I'm defining the engine cylinders from the crankcase position angling outward and upward.

Still working out cylinder geometry...

Actually I realize the front downtube path intersects the front cylinder around y=.7 — I need to reroute it so it sweeps forward and down toward the footplate, clearing the engine entirely, matching how the reference frame curves in front of the motor.

Still placing frame tubes...

Still working out positions...

I'm connecting the rail to the axle via a link rod, keeping rails stable at x ±.15, then applying the same approach to the seat stays and checking their height against the tire's outer radius at z -.5 to avoid overlap.

Checking the stay geometry more closely at z -.6, the clearance to the tire comes out tight but just barely clears, so I'll use top x ±.13 with axle ±.15 as the safe values, and confirm rear fender width spans fine.

Now I'm placing the seat, making sure its bottom sits flush on the backbone rather than floating above it.

Working through the rear fender's curvature to check it clears the seat bottom with a small gap, and tracing the fender's front edge position relative to the seat.

For the footpegs, I'm checking whether the mounting rod would physically intersect the exhaust pipe's path, since both occupy similar x/y/z space near the rear of the bike.

I'm settling on forward-control-style pegs positioned further ahead at a higher z, keeping clear of the exhaust route, with simple black rubber cylinder pegs mounted on steel rods extending outward from the frame.

Skipping the shifter for now and adding a kickstand as a bone joint pivoting from the lower frame down to a small foot, plus mirror stems attached to the handlebars with octahedron-shaped mirror heads, and brake/clutch levers mounted near the bar ends aiming forward.

Working out lever and grip positions...

Still orienting fork tube geometry...

For the fuel tank, I'm thinking through gradient paint options and whether sectors can override base color, then working out how to attach the tank loft to the frame bone correctly.

Since joints default to the nearest position, I need to explicitly assign bones for each part to avoid misattachment—steer joint at the head, wheelF parented to steer, wheelR and kickstand parented to frame, plus lever joints. I'll write small helper functions to pass geometry, color, bone, and position consistently, and assign hinge roles to the steering and wheel joints for the chain setup.

Now I'm deciding on decal details—maybe a hex badge on the tank and a stripe panel on the engine rather than overdoing arrow chevrons—then setting up the imports I'll need (THREE, geometry merging, builder, path curves, paint/gradient, texture, glow, and the Joint type) while being careful to avoid any unused imports under strict TypeScript settings.

Writing geometry helper functions...

Continuing to define the remaining joints...

Then I'm setting up a helper function to simplify attaching mesh parts to bones at specific local positions, so I can call it concisely for each body piece.

Now I'm defining a wheel function that paints tire tread patterns and orange sidewall rings based on radial distance from the wheel's center and surface normal direction.

Still building wheel geometry...

Adding tiny dark cylinders...

Building the seat loft stations with varying width and height profiles, including a raised backrest bump near the rear, plus fender trim details and an orange hexagonal badge extruded as a thin flat shape.

Checking the tank's cross-section widths against the hex badge position so it pokes out slightly from the surface, and considering a smaller inner teal-dark hex layered on top for contrast.

Adding engine details...

Skipping pushrod tubes and spark plugs for simplicity; now I'm working out exhaust header paths starting from the front cylinder's port position and routing down the side of the bike.

For the muffler shape, I'm defining a radius function that stays thin near the header then abruptly widens with a smooth lerp transition around the midpoint, tapering again near the tip, colored chrome. I'm also starting the shorter rear cylinder exhaust pipe path.

Placing orange exhaust rings along the muffler path and adjusting foot pegs on both sides so they align near the exhaust segment positions.

Working out the frame tube's downtube and cradle geometry...

I'm checking for collisions between the exhaust pipe and the rail rods near the crankcase, and adjusting the exhaust's x-position further out to avoid overlap with the rail at that section.

For the drivetrain, I'm placing the sprockets so they sit inside the hub region rather than colliding with the rails or tire—since the tire's inner radius leaves room for a smaller-radius sprocket near the axle.

I keep adjusting positions: moving rails to x ±.18 and both engine and rear sprockets to x .13 so the chain line, crankcase, and primary cover all clear each other without overlap.

Then I'm placing primary cover on the right side with the chain-drive on the left, checking that the exhaust pipe at y .3 doesn't collide with the cover's lower edge — nudging cover y up to .46 to get clean clearance, and confirming the pickup coil sits fine on the right while the air cleaner occupies the left.

Switching plan: primary cover goes on the left (more visible), chain and sprockets move to the right alongside the exhaust, checking that the exhaust at x -.27 clears the chain centered at x -.13. I'm working out sprocket positions — engine sprocket near [-.13, .4, -.12] with r .05, and rear sprocket further back at [-.13, WY, -.7] with r .1 — to define the chain run between them.

Verifying clearances...

Adding a cross rod under the seat connecting the backbone end to the rear stays, then rounding out the part count with small dressing details like frame bolts and reflectors, plus a rear license plate decal.

Deciding to skip reflector decals and instead add orange paint accent bands along the downtube using a band-splitting color list, then moving on to write the file with proper TypeScript outline types and checking rotation/quaternion options for the fender part, including setting up a quaternion helper for the partial torus fender.

Working out the fender geometry as a partial torus with an orange trim stripe sitting just outside the main fender radius, tuning the arc length and offsets so the stripe reads as a thin accent line, then planning to apply the same treatment to the rear fender and mirrors before writing it all out.

Now I'm adding support stays connecting the fenders to the frame, computing attachment angles and positions so the front fender stay runs from the axle block up to a point near its top edge, and doing the same for the rear fender tying into the seat stay area.

Next I'm setting up the steering joint configuration and defining the color palette constants for the frame, tires, seat, and metal parts.

Now I'm adding the tail light glow box and headlight lens, using a circle geometry with a grid-patterned SVG texture for the lens detail.

Working out the headlight lens placement, I'm recessing it slightly within the rim torus and making sure the circle geometry faces outward correctly along the z-axis without needing extra rotation. I'm also sketching out a dark speedometer dial texture and double-checking the catmull-rom spline typing for the body sweep curve.

For the fork, I'm setting up a two-point sweep path bound to the steering bone with flat caps, mirrored across both sides.
